Pregnancy

Postmortem after stillbirth: choices and understanding results

Updated: November 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

After a stillbirth, you may be asked whether you want a postmortem examination of your baby. Facing this decision while grieving can be very difficult. You deserve an explanation of what the examination involves, what it might answer and which alternatives are available. This guide concerns examination after a baby has died before birth; a small tissue test after an early miscarriage is a different investigation.

A postmortem is one part of a wider review

A postmortem, also called an autopsy, is an examination after death by a specialist doctor called a pathologist. A perinatal pathologist has particular expertise in babies and pregnancy-related tissues. The examination is considered alongside pregnancy records, scans, the circumstances of the loss, maternal tests and examination of the placenta, cord and membranes.

A biopsy means taking a small tissue sample. Examining that sample under a microscope is different from testing its chromosomes or genes, and neither is the same as a complete postmortem. Ask your team to name each proposed investigation and explain its purpose. Agreeing to one test should not leave you uncertain about what else is planned.

What useful information could it provide?

The findings may support a suspected explanation, identify a previously unrecognised condition or make a particular cause less likely. They can sometimes change advice about future care. The value depends on the circumstances, the examinations completed and how their findings fit together. A normal scan during pregnancy does not make examination after death automatically unhelpful.

There is no single percentage that predicts whether your family will receive an answer. Studies count different things: a definite cause, a possible contribution or any additional information. Results from a full investigation cannot be attributed to the autopsy alone. Ask what the pathologist may be able to clarify in your baby's particular case, including what is likely to remain uncertain.

What happens in a full examination?

The pathologist reviews the clinical information and examines the baby's body externally, including measurements and any physical differences. A full examination also involves careful incisions and inspection of internal organs. Small tissue samples may be examined microscopically, with other tests selected when appropriate. Clinical photographs or imaging may form part of the assessment; ask what is proposed.

The body is carefully repaired afterward. Ask who will perform the examination, where your baby will be cared for and whether transfer to another centre is needed. Examination of the placenta can provide information about the pregnancy that examination of the baby alone cannot. Genetic tests may also contribute, but their possible findings and consent need explanation.

Full examination is not the only possible option

A limited postmortem examines agreed areas or organs. An external examination looks at the outside of the body; imaging or separately agreed sampling may add information. Some centres offer postmortem MRI, ultrasound or minimally invasive tissue sampling. These options vary with local expertise, the baby's size and condition, and the question being investigated.

An imaging study cannot reveal everything that examination of tissue under a microscope can show. Conversely, a particular scan may be useful for a specific suspected problem. Ask which alternatives are available and what information could be lost by limiting the examination. If you decline examination of the baby's internal organs, placental assessment and other agreed tests may still be useful.

Make the consent discussion specific

For an ordinary hospital postmortem offered to investigate a stillbirth, the team should explain the choices and obtain the required consent. Ask for a trained professional, written information, an interpreter if needed and time to consider your questions. You can ask for less detail initially and return to the discussion. The form should clearly describe the permitted extent of examination.

Ask when a decision is needed, whether any delay affects the available tests, and whom to contact if you change your mind. Do not assume every hospital has the same reconsideration period. Legally required investigations follow different rules that depend on the jurisdiction and circumstances. If that applies, ask the local team to explain the process and your options; a general article cannot establish the legal position.

Discuss retained samples and research separately

Small pieces of tissue may be processed into blocks and microscope slides that become part of the medical record. Other samples may be stored for further testing, and occasionally an organ needs longer examination. These are different arrangements. Ask what may be retained, why, for how long, and what choices you have about its eventual return or disposal.

Clarify which permissions cover clinical investigation and which cover research, teaching or other uses. You should understand these choices rather than assume that agreeing to an examination means agreeing to every future use. Ask how your preferences are recorded and request a copy. If genetic testing is proposed, discuss its limits and the possibility of information relevant to other family members.

Planning time with your baby and the funeral

It is often possible to see or hold your baby after the examination, and incisions are usually covered when the baby is dressed. However, appearance also changes naturally after death, and very small or fragile babies may need particular care. Ask the bereavement team what to expect and whether spending time together before the examination would be advisable in your circumstances.

A postmortem does not itself prevent a funeral, but transport, the examination and decisions about retained organs can affect timing. Ask when your baby is expected to return and which arrangements can be made before then. The final laboratory report may take much longer than the examination itself. Discuss any important timing preferences without assuming that a particular date can be guaranteed.

Getting the report and having it explained

The report may describe the baby's measurements and appearance, examination of organs and tissues, placental findings and results of additional tests. It should help the clinical team explain what was found and how confidently those findings relate to the death. Technical terms or an abnormal result should be discussed with someone who knows the whole pregnancy history.

Results can take weeks or months, especially when additional tests or specialist opinions are needed. Ask for the local estimate, a named contact for updates and a follow-up appointment. Find out whether preliminary findings are available and how to obtain a copy or plain-language summary. You can bring someone you trust and ask for another conversation if the first discussion is too much to absorb.

An uncertain result still needs a careful conversation

Sometimes no definite cause is found despite a thorough examination. That does not mean nothing happened, nor does it establish that a parent did something wrong. Ask whether the report identifies a likely cause, a possible contributor or a finding whose significance is unclear. A result that does not support one suspected condition cannot rule out every genetic or medical explanation.

If you want another pregnancy, the findings may guide genetic counselling, treatment of a relevant health condition or an individual monitoring plan. They cannot guarantee prevention of another loss or a healthy future birth. Ask which recommendation follows from which finding, and what advice remains appropriate when the cause is unknown. Wanting information is also valid if you do not plan another pregnancy.

Questions can help you make your own choice

You might ask: what are the most important unanswered questions, which examination could address them, and what would each possible result change? Also ask about the practical arrangements, available alternatives and any costs. Tell the team which concern matters most to you, whether it is understanding the death, the examination itself, time with your baby or waiting for results.

You and your partner may want different amounts of information or feel differently about the decision. A bereavement professional can help you talk through those concerns and explain who needs to give consent locally. Neither agreeing nor declining proves how much you love your baby. Staff should support an informed decision without promising emotional closure or predicting that you will regret a particular choice.

Support continues while you wait

You can ask for bereavement support before deciding, while results are pending and after the follow-up appointment. Grief does not have to end when the report arrives, and support should not depend on whether a cause is found. Let your maternity team or usual clinician know if distress is making daily life difficult. Your physical recovery also needs care during this period.

Get medical help immediately for fever, worsening abdominal pain, foul-smelling discharge or a severe persistent headache after birth. Heavy bleeding, fainting or collapse, chest pain or difficulty breathing needs emergency assessment. Tell the service that you recently gave birth. If you feel unable to keep yourself safe or may act on thoughts of self-harm, seek emergency help and ask someone you trust to stay with you.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Interpret the postmortem alongside pregnancy history, placental findings and other appropriate tests.

Discuss the extent of examination, alternatives, retention and result communication before deciding.

Use local service information for timing and legal processes; no single yield or recurrence estimate fits every family.

How BeMama can help

Use this guide to prepare questions for your maternity and bereavement teams. BeMama cannot interpret an individual pathology report, determine the cause of a loss or give consent on your behalf.

When to seek help

After birth, fever, worsening pain, foul discharge or a severe persistent headache needs immediate medical attention. Heavy bleeding, fainting, chest pain, breathing difficulty or inability to stay safe requires emergency help; do not wait for postmortem results.

Evidence notes updated: November 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A postmortem is a specialist examination, distinct from a single tissue sample or chromosome test.
  • Ask about the likely value and limits of full, limited and locally available less invasive options.
  • Clarify consent, retained samples, genetic testing and research permissions separately.
  • Discuss viewing, transport, funeral timing and how results will be communicated.
  • An examination may guide future care, but cannot promise a cause, prevention or emotional closure.

Frequently asked questions

Could a postmortem help me understand why my baby died?

It may confirm a suspected explanation, identify something previously unknown or narrow the possibilities. Its value depends on your baby's circumstances and the other investigations. Ask what questions it could answer for your family; a study percentage cannot predict an individual result.

Can we still arrange a funeral afterward?

Yes, but the examination, transport or a decision to wait for retained organs may affect timing. Ask when your baby can be returned and which arrangements can proceed. Waiting for the final report is different from waiting for the examination to finish.

What information will the report contain?

It can describe external and internal findings, measurements, tissue and placental examination, and additional test results. Your clinician should explain how these relate to the pregnancy and which conclusions are certain or uncertain. Ask for a copy and a plain-language discussion.

Will a postmortem always find the cause?

No. Some losses remain unexplained even after extensive investigation. An inconclusive result does not exclude every possible inherited condition or predict the chance of another loss. Ask what has become less likely and how the findings affect your care.

What if I do not want a full examination?

Ask about a limited or external examination, imaging or minimally invasive sampling where available. Placental examination and other agreed tests may still help. The team should explain what each option could answer and what it might miss, without implying that all options provide identical information.

Do I have to agree to research if I agree to the examination?

Research and teaching uses should be explained as separate choices within the consent discussion. Ask which permissions cover clinical testing and retention, and which cover other uses. Request a record of your preferences and contact details if you have further questions.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
